paragraphs.heading: The flourishing town
paragraphs.text: Florence, called Firenze in Italian, is the capital and largest city of Tuscany. The Romans founded it in 59 BC as a settlement for veteran soldiers, laid out like an army camp. Its Latin name, Florentia, means "the Flourishing Town", from a verb meaning to flourish or blossom. The modern name Firenze grew out of that ancient one.

paragraphs.heading: A river and a road
paragraphs.text: The town sat on the Via Cassia, the main road from Rome to the north, in the fertile valley of the river Arno, and it soon became a busy place of trade. Later the Arno powered local industry, mostly textiles, and gave merchants a route to the Mediterranean. By 1100 Florence was a commune, which meant a city-state.

paragraphs.heading: Bankers to Europe
paragraphs.text: In the Middle Ages Florence became one of Europe's richest cities and a center of trade and finance. Its merchant bankers brought new tools to the trade fairs, such as bills of exchange and double-entry bookkeeping. Its gold coin, the florin, paid for industry from Britain and Bruges to Lyon and Hungary. Florentine bankers lent to the English kings during the Hundred Years' War and to the popes as well.

paragraphs.heading: Cradle of the Renaissance
paragraphs.text: Many scholars see Florence as the place where the Renaissance was born. From the 14th to the 16th centuries it was among the most important cities in Europe and the world, in politics, money and culture alike. Its influence spread across Italy, Europe and beyond.

paragraphs.heading: The Medici
paragraphs.text: Florence was home to the Medici, one of the most important noble families in European history. In the late 15th century, Lorenzo de' Medici was regarded as a mastermind of Italian politics and culture. In the early 16th century the family gave the Church two popes, Leo X and Clement VII. Later the family ruled as Grand Dukes of Tuscany from 1569 until 1737.

paragraphs.heading: The language of Italy
paragraphs.text: One lasting gift of Florence is the Italian language itself. The speech of 14th-century Florence became the model for it. The great works of the Tuscan writers Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio gave the Florentine dialect such prestige that it was taken up as the basis for a national literary language.

paragraphs.heading: Florence today
paragraphs.text: The city is still known for its Renaissance art, buildings and monuments. It draws millions of tourists each year, and its many museums and galleries include the Uffizi and the Palazzo Pitti. In 1982 UNESCO named its historic center a World Heritage Site.
